A Fixed Universal Determinant is Variationally Complete for Continuum Fermions

Giuseppe Carleo Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland Affiliation: Center for Quantum Science and Engineering, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland    Riccardo Rossi Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland Affiliation: Center for Quantum Science and Engineering, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland Affiliation: CNRS, Laboratoire de Physique Théorique de la Matière Condensée, Sorbonne Université, 75005 Paris, France
August 24, 2026
Abstract

How many Slater determinants does an accurate variational description of interacting fermions require? Exact expansions in a finite basis need combinatorially many, and state-of-the-art fermionic neural quantum states stack growing numbers of them. We prove that, in the norms that govern variational calculations, at most two are needed, independently of the number of particles and of the target accuracy. A single universal Slater determinant—specified in advance, independent of both the system and the state—multiplied by a smooth bosonic wave function approximates any fermionic wave function in up to three spatial dimensions in the first-order Sobolev norm, which controls the variational energy. Reaching the second-order Sobolev norm—for Coulomb interactions, the domain of the Hamiltonian, which bounds the variance of the local energy at the core of variational Monte Carlo—requires at most one additional fixed determinant, and only in three dimensions. Antisymmetry therefore costs at most two universal determinants and no expressiveness: generalized Slater–Jastrow neural quantum states are variationally complete.

Neural quantum states and expressivity.—Interacting fermions, from electrons in molecules and solids to dense nuclear matter, are the central and hardest instance of the quantum many-body problem: the Pauli principle forces the wave function to change sign under particle exchange, and building this antisymmetry into an expressive variational family has been a structural challenge of many-body physics for decades, from Slater–Jastrow and backflow trial states [9, 25, 5, 20] to the nodal surfaces that control fixed-node quantum Monte Carlo [30, 6, 10]. Neural quantum states (NQS) parametrize the amplitude of each many-body configuration directly with a network [3, 2], and a substantial representation theory has since developed: bounds on the entanglement an architecture can support, constructions of volume-law and tensor-network states, and universality results relating network depth to expressive power [12, 8, 21, 32]. On a lattice, antisymmetry is naturally carried by the second-quantized fermionic algebra through Jordan–Wigner strings or a reference determinant in an occupation basis [26, 7]. In the continuum, the state of NN spinless fermions in dd spatial dimensions is instead a first-quantized antisymmetric wave function on ℝd×N\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}. In NQS, the antisymmetry is usually supplied by combining a permutation-equivariant network with explicit antisymmetric objects, typically Slater determinants or Pfaffians [24, 29, 15, 33, 4, 23, 27, 16, 19, 31, 28].

How many antisymmetric blocks are then unavoidable? The answer depends sharply on the notion of approximation and on what is allowed as a block (Table 1). Exact expansions in a finite basis require combinatorially many determinants, and a single generalized backflow determinant can represent any fermionic wave function exactly only at the price of orbitals that are discontinuous for d>1d>1 and target dependent [17]. For uniform pointwise approximation with continuous factors the cost remains steep: K=O⁡(ϵ−N​d)K=O(\epsilon^{-Nd}) backflow–Vandermonde terms at accuracy ϵ\epsilon [14], and K=d​N+1K=dN+1 fixed determinants for an exact continuous representation [34], a count reduced by Fu’s Fermi Sets to K=1K=1 in d=1d=1, K=2K=2 in d=2d=2, and K≤d​N+1K\leq dN+1 for d≥3d\geq 3 [11]. The obstruction is geometric: a fixed determinant carries an artificial nodal surface that no continuous bosonic factor can cure uniformly.

Uniform approximation is, however, different than what physics requires: the supremum norm constrains the amplitude at every configuration, while energies and observables are integrals over particle positions involving as integrand the value of the wave function and of the derivatives. More natural settings for variational calculations are instead Sobolev spaces. For a Coulomb Hamiltonian in three dimensions, the quadratic form of the energy is defined on the first-order Sobolev space H1​(ℝd×N)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}) [22], and the operator domain is the second-order space H2​(ℝd×N)H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}) [18], whose norm controls the variance of the local energy, the central estimator of variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [25, 5, 10]. It is in these topologies that the fermionic variational representation question should be posed.

In this Letter we prove that, in the Sobolev norms, the cost of antisymmetry collapses. For d≤3d\leq 3, a single fixed, universal complex Slater determinant multiplied by a smooth compactly-supported bosonic wave function is dense in the fermionic H1H^{1} space; in H2H^{2}, one determinant suffices for d≤2d\leq 2 and at most two for d=3d=3 (Table 1). These counts are independent of the particle number and of the target accuracy: a growing determinant expansion is unnecessary for variational completeness, and the entire expressive burden can be carried by one—at the H2H^{2} level, at most two—bosonic wave functions. For neural quantum states, the construction amounts to a generalized Slater–Jastrow wave function whose Jastrow factor is sign indefinite and not restricted to few-body correlations.

Wave function spaces. For simplicity of discussion, we restrict ourselves here to spinless particles. The extension to spinful particles is straightforward and discussed later. We consider NN particles in dd spatial dimensions, described by square-integrable wave functions ψ⁡(𝒓1,…,𝒓N)\psi(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N}) on ℝd×N\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}, forming the space L2​(ℝd×N)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}). Particle statistics selects a subspace, indicated by a ±\pm subscript: fermionic wave functions are antisymmetric under particle permutations and form L−2L^{2}_{-}, bosonic ones are symmetric and form L+2L^{2}_{+}. The continuous-space Hamiltonian is H=∑i=1N[−ℏ22​m​∇i2+Vext​(𝐫i)]+12​∑i≠jU⁡(𝐫i−𝐫j)H=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla_{i}^{2}+V_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r}_{i})\right]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\neq j}U(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}), where UU denotes the two-body Coulomb interaction and VextV_{\text{ext}} a one-body potential. Wave functions of finite average kinetic energy form the first-order Sobolev space H−1​(ℝd×N)H^{1}_{-}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}) which, in three dimensions and under mild assumptions on VextV_{\text{ext}}, is also the space of finite average energy [22]. The domain D⁡(H)D(H) on which the Hamiltonian itself is defined coincides in three dimensions with the second-order Sobolev space, for fermions H−2​(ℝd×N)H^{2}_{-}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}): the functions of H−1H^{1}_{-} with square-integrable Laplacian [18]. The Hamiltonian domain is not a mere technicality in VMC practice: the main Monte Carlo estimator is the local energy

Eloc​(𝒓1,…,𝒓N)=(H​ψ)​(𝒓1,…,𝒓N)ψ⁡(𝒓1,…,𝒓N),E_{\text{loc}}(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N})=\frac{(H\psi)(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N})}{\psi(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N})}, (1)

and ψ∈H2\psi\in H^{2} guarantees that its Monte Carlo variance is bounded. H1H^{1} and H2H^{2} are the two Sobolev norms in which we pose, and answer, the fermionic representation question.

For neural-network architectures optimized with gradient methods, working with smooth functions subject to no antisymmetry constraint is a practical necessity. We denote by Cc∞C^{\infty}_{c} the set of compactly-supported smooth functions. We will use the well-known fact that Cc∞​(ℝd×N)C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}) is dense in Hs​(ℝd×N)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}) in the HsH^{s} norm [1]. We can now state the main result of this work.

Theorem 1.

Let s∈{1,2}s\in\{1,2\} and d≤3d\leq 3, and let ψ∈H−s​(ℝd×N)\psi\in H^{s}_{-}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}) be a spinless fermionic wave function of NN particles in dd spatial dimensions. Then there exist sequences of smooth compactly-supported bosonic NN-particle wave functions ϕα,n∈Cc,+∞​(ℝd×N)\phi_{\alpha,n}\in C^{\infty}_{c,+}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}) such that

limn→∞‖ψ−∑α=1Ks(d)𝒟α(d)​ϕα,n‖Hs=0,\lim_{n\to\infty}\left\lVert\psi-\sum_{\alpha=1}^{K_{s}^{(d)}}\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}^{(d)}\,\phi_{\alpha,n}\right\rVert_{H^{s}}=0, (2)

where the 𝒟α(d)\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}^{(d)} are universal, ψ\psi-independent, antisymmetric polynomials in the particle coordinates, and where K1(d)=1K_{1}^{(d)}=1 for d∈{1,2,3}d\in\{1,2,3\}, K2(d)=1K_{2}^{(d)}=1 for d∈{1,2}d\in\{1,2\}, and K2(3)≤2K_{2}^{(3)}\leq 2.

The complete proof of Theorem 1 is presented in the Supplemental Material, while below we sketch the main conceptual steps. After introducing the main objects of the proof, we first discuss the H1H^{1} case and then show the modifications needed to establish the H2H^{2} variant. Finally, we note at the end that the theorem is also applicable to the spinful case without modification.

Construction of the universal determinants. We give below the explicit expression of the fixed Slater determinants 𝒟α(d)\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}^{(d)}, which are all of the Vandermonde form. Let 𝒩α(d)\mathcal{N}_{\alpha}^{(d)} be the set of zeros of 𝒟α(d)\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}^{(d)}, which we refer to as the nodal surface. We also introduce the collision nodal surface 𝒩c(d)\mathcal{N}_{c}^{(d)}, which is the set of points where two or more particles share the same position and where any continuous fermionic wave function must vanish.

For d=1d=1 it is sufficient to consider the real determinant

𝒟1(1)​(𝒓1,…,𝒓N)=∏j<k(xk−xj)=det(xjk−1)j,k=1N.\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(1)}(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N})=\prod_{j<k}(x_{k}-x_{j})=\det\big(x_{j}^{\,k-1}\big)_{j,k=1}^{N}. (3)

The theorem is particularly simple to motivate in one dimension using the 𝒟1(1)\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(1)} antisymmetric factor: as 𝒩1(1)≡𝒩c(1)\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(1)}\equiv\mathcal{N}_{c}^{(1)}, any smooth antisymmetric function ψn∈Cc,−∞\psi_{n}\in C^{\infty}_{c,-} approximating ψ∈H−s\psi\in H^{s}_{-} can be safely divided by 𝒟1(1)\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(1)}, providing another smooth symmetric function ϕ1,n=ψn𝒟1(1)∈Cc,+∞\phi_{1,n}=\frac{\psi_{n}}{\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(1)}}\in C^{\infty}_{c,+}. This result is perhaps not surprising in view of the long history of fermion-boson mappings in one dimension [13].

For d>1d>1, we introduce the complex determinant

𝒟1(d)​(𝒓1,…,𝒓N)=∏j<k(ζk−ζj)=det(ζjk−1)\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(d)}(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N})=\prod_{j<k}(\zeta_{k}-\zeta_{j})=\det\big(\zeta_{j}^{\,k-1}\big) (4)

where ζj=xj+i​yj∈ℂ\zeta_{j}=x_{j}+iy_{j}\in\mathbb{C}, and for d=3d=3 we define an additional complex determinant

𝒟2(3)​(𝒓1,…,𝒓N)=∏j<k(ξk−ξj)=det(ξjk−1),\mathcal{D}_{2}^{(3)}(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N})=\prod_{j<k}(\xi_{k}-\xi_{j})=\det\big(\xi_{j}^{\,k-1}\big), (5)

where ξj=yj+i​zj∈ℂ\xi_{j}=y_{j}+iz_{j}\in\mathbb{C}. These forms of Slater determinants were also considered in previous works [34, 11].

The 𝒩1(d)\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(d)} nodal surface. We focus here on 𝒩1(d)\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(d)} for d>1d>1, which is the union of 𝒩1;(j,k)(d)\mathcal{N}_{1;(j,k)}^{(d)} for all pairs of particles (j,k)(j,k)

𝒩1;(j,k)(d)={(𝒓1,…,𝒓N)∈ℝd×N|xj=xk,yj=yk},\mathcal{N}_{1;(j,k)}^{(d)}=\left\{(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}\,\Big|\,x_{j}=x_{k},\;y_{j}=y_{k}\right\}, (6)

which is a vector subspace of codimension q=2q=2.

Introducing the cutoff function for 𝒩1(d)\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(d)}. The central device of the proof is a smooth cutoff that deletes the artificial nodal surface at vanishing Sobolev cost. We introduce χϵ∈C∞\chi_{\epsilon}\in C^{\infty}, identically zero near 𝒩1(d)\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(d)} and converging to 11 everywhere expect the nodal surface as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0. Let ρ⁡(𝒓1,…,𝒓N)\rho(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N}) be a smooth version of the minimal distance of (𝒓1,…,𝒓N)(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N}) from 𝒩1(d)\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(d)}. We choose the cutoff function χϵ\chi_{\epsilon} to be a function of ρ\rho, and to be equal to 11 for ρ≥ϵ\rho\geq\epsilon. We remark that, as the nodal surface 𝒩1(d)\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(d)} is symmetric, the cutoff function can be chosen symmetric, χϵ∈C+∞\chi_{\epsilon}\in C^{\infty}_{+}. Loosely speaking, χϵ\chi_{\epsilon} must not have a large gradient, as this might spoil the H1H^{1} convergence. Crucially, it turns out that one can choose χϵ\chi_{\epsilon} that satisfies the bounds |χϵ′​(ρ)|≤Clog⁡ϵ−1​ρ|\chi_{\epsilon}^{\prime}(\rho)|\leq\frac{C}{\log\epsilon^{-1}\;\rho}, |χϵ′′​(ρ)|≤Clog⁡ϵ−1​ρ2|\chi_{\epsilon}^{\prime\prime}(\rho)|\leq\frac{C}{\log\epsilon^{-1}\,\rho^{2}}, and such that χϵ​(ρ)=0\chi_{\epsilon}(\rho)=0 for ρ≤ϵ2\rho\leq\epsilon^{2}. These bounds follow directly from the choice χϵ​(ρ)=θ⁡(log⁡τϵ)\chi_{\epsilon}(\rho)=\theta(\log\tau_{\epsilon}), where τϵ=(ρϵ2)1log⁡ϵ−1\tau_{\epsilon}=\left(\frac{\rho}{\epsilon^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{\log\epsilon^{-1}}}, and where θ\theta is a smooth function that goes from zero to one in [0,1][0,1].

The deletion lemma for the H1H^{1} case.—The essential lemma we use in the proof states that if u∈Cc∞u\in C^{\infty}_{c}, then u​χϵ→uu\chi_{\epsilon}\to u in H1H^{1}. To prove it, let us first remark that u−u​χϵu-u\chi_{\epsilon} is clearly in L2L^{2}, while the gradient reads

‖∇(u−u​χϵ)‖2≤‖∇u​(1−χϵ)‖2+‖u‖∞||∇χϵ||L2​(S),||\nabla(u-u\chi_{\epsilon})||_{2}\leq||\nabla\,u\;(1-\chi_{\epsilon})||_{2}+||u||_{\infty}\,||\nabla\chi_{\epsilon}||_{L^{2}(S)}, (7)

where SS is the support of uu. The first term vanishes as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 by dominated convergence, as 1−χϵ→01-\chi_{\epsilon}\to 0 almost everywhere and is bounded by one. The only potentially-problematic term therefore comes from the norm of the gradient of the cutoff function on the compact support of uu,

‖∇χϵ‖L2​(S)2∼∫ϵ2ϵd​ρ​ρq−1​|χϵ′|2≤C(log⁡ϵ−1)2​∫ϵ2ϵd​ρ​ρq−3,||\nabla\chi_{\epsilon}||_{L^{2}(S)}^{2}\sim\int_{\epsilon^{2}}^{\epsilon}d\rho\,\rho^{q-1}|\chi^{\prime}_{\epsilon}|^{2}\leq\frac{C}{(\log\epsilon^{-1})^{2}}\int_{\epsilon^{2}}^{\epsilon}d\rho\,\rho^{q-3}, (8)

where the factor ρq−1\rho^{q-1} comes from the Jacobian for the change of variable to the ρ\rho coordinate, and where qq is the codimension of the subspace 𝒩1;(j,k)(d)\mathcal{N}_{1;(j,k)}^{(d)} (see Fig. 1b for a sketch). The norm of the gradient of χϵ\chi_{\epsilon} therefore goes to zero for ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 for q≥2q\geq 2. We also see why using 𝒟1(1)\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(1)} evaluated on a single Cartesian coordinate would not have been enough for d>1d>1: the corresponding nodal surface is made of codimension-one subspaces (see Fig. 1(a) for a sketch).

Assembling the proof for the H1H^{1} case.—Let ψn∈Cc,−∞\psi_{n}\in C^{\infty}_{c,-} be a sequence converging to ψ∈H−1\psi\in H^{1}_{-} with ‖ψ−ψn‖H1≤1n||\psi-\psi_{n}||_{H^{1}}\leq\frac{1}{n}. Let ψn,m=χ1m​ψn∈Cc,−∞\psi_{n,m}=\chi_{\frac{1}{m}}\,\psi_{n}\in C^{\infty}_{c,-}. By the deletion lemma, ψn,m→ψn\psi_{n,m}\to\psi_{n} in H1H^{1} when m→∞m\to\infty. Let m⁡(n)m(n) be such that ‖ψn−ψn,m⁡(n)‖H1≤1n||\psi_{n}-\psi_{n,m(n)}||_{H^{1}}\leq\frac{1}{n}. Define

ϕ1,n=ψn,m⁡(n)𝒟1(d)∈Cc,+∞.\phi_{1,n}=\frac{\psi_{n,m(n)}}{\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(d)}}\in C^{\infty}_{c,+}. (9)

Then, ‖ψ−𝒟1(d)​ϕ1,n‖H1≤2n||\psi-\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(d)}\,\phi_{1,n}||_{H^{1}}\leq\frac{2}{n}, which shows that ψ\psi can be approximated in the first-order Sobolev norm by a generalized Slater-Jastrow wave function (see Fig. 1(c)).

Extension to the H2H^{2} case.—It is possible to extend the deletion lemma above to show convergence of u​χϵu\chi_{\epsilon} to uu in H2H^{2} if the minimal codimension of the subspaces of the nodal surface is q≥4q\geq 4. 𝒩1(d)\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(d)} is made of subspaces of codimension q=2q=2, so the lemma is not directly applicable.

We first consider d=2d=2. In this case, 𝒩1(2)\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(2)} coincides with the collision nodal surface 𝒩c(2)\mathcal{N}_{c}^{(2)}, which means that the wave function must be zero there. If a smooth function is zero on the nodal surface, a variant of the deletion lemma in H2H^{2} decreases the minimal codimension to q≥2q\geq 2, which concludes the proof of the two-dimensional case.

In the three-dimensional case, we are led to consider the two complex determinants 𝒟1(3)\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(3)} and 𝒟2(3)\mathcal{D}_{2}^{(3)}. We focus on the intersection of the nodal surfaces 𝒩1(3)\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(3)} and 𝒩2(3)\mathcal{N}_{2}^{(3)} of the two determinants, 𝒩(3)12=∪e,e′∈ℰLe,e′\mathcal{N}^{(3)}_{12}=\cup_{e,e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}}\,L_{e,e^{\prime}}, where ℰ\mathcal{E} is the set of pairs of particles, and L(j,k),(j′,k′)={(𝒓1,…,𝒓N)∈ℝd×N|ζj=ζk,ξj′=ξk′}L_{(j,k),(j^{\prime},k^{\prime})}=\{(\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{N})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}|\zeta_{j}=\zeta_{k},\;\xi_{j^{\prime}}=\xi_{k^{\prime}}\} (see Fig. 2 for a sketch). Le,eL_{e,e} has codimension q=3q=3, and it is contained in the collision nodal surface, which means that we can apply the variant of the deletion lemma with minimal codimension q=2q=2. Le,e′L_{e,e^{\prime}} with e≠e′e\neq e^{\prime} has codimension q=4q=4. We can therefore conclude that u​χϵ→uu\chi_{\epsilon}\to u in H2H^{2} for every u∈Cc∞u\in C^{\infty}_{c} and for a smooth χϵ\chi_{\epsilon} that is zero near 𝒩12(3)\mathcal{N}_{12}^{(3)}. For ψn∈Cc,−∞\psi_{n}\in C^{\infty}_{c,-} converging towards ψ∈H−2\psi\in H^{2}_{-}, we define, similarly to what was done for the H1H^{1} case

ϕα,n=χ1m⁡(n)​[𝒟α(3)]∗​ψn|𝒟1(3)|2+|𝒟2(3)|2∈Cc,+∞,\phi_{\alpha,n}=\chi_{\frac{1}{m(n)}}\;\frac{[\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}^{(3)}]^{*}\,\psi_{n}}{|\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(3)}|^{2}+|\mathcal{D}_{2}^{(3)}|^{2}}\in C^{\infty}_{c,+}, (10)

which is a smooth function as it is identically zero by construction near the problematic set 𝒟1(3)=𝒟2(3)=0\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(3)}=\mathcal{D}_{2}^{(3)}=0. This concludes the presentation of the proof of Theorem 1.

Extension to the spinful case. We consider a fixed number NσN_{\sigma} of spin-σ\sigma particles, for σ∈{↑,↓}\sigma\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}. The fermionic wave function is antisymmetric in the coordinates for the spin-up and spin-down particle separately. Accordingly, it is sufficient to define the determinants as the products of determinants for the spin-up and the spin-down particles separately

𝒟α(d)​(𝑹↑,𝑹↓)=𝒟α(d)​(𝑹↑)​𝒟α(d)​(𝑹↓),\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}^{(d)}(\bm{R}_{\uparrow},\bm{R}_{\downarrow})=\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}^{(d)}(\bm{R}_{\uparrow})\;\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}^{(d)}(\bm{R}_{\downarrow}), (11)

where 𝑹σ=(𝒓1,σ,…,𝒓Nσ,σ)\bm{R}_{\sigma}=(\bm{r}_{1,\sigma},\dots,\bm{r}_{N_{\sigma},\sigma}), and the determinant count Ks(d)K_{s}^{(d)} is identical to the spinless case.

Discussion.—Theorem 1 provides a representation-theoretic baseline for continuum fermionic variational calculations: at the level of the variational energy, a single fixed Vandermonde determinant multiplied by a smooth bosonic factor already spans the whole fermionic H1H^{1} space; controlling the local energy—hence the Monte Carlo variance—requires at most one additional determinant, and only in three dimensions. The number of explicitly antisymmetric objects is therefore not a source of expressiveness for neural quantum states: a single-determinant generalized Slater–Jastrow ansatz with a sufficiently flexible bosonic network is variationally complete, and additional determinants or Pfaffian factors should be understood as improving the conditioning of the bosonic factor near the artificial nodal surfaces rather than enlarging the reachable state space. We note however that the theorem is silent on optimization: the exact factors ϕα,n\phi_{\alpha,n} must reconstruct the true nodal structure of the wave function, and quantifying the difficulty of this task—together with approximation rates as a function of NN—remains an open problem.

End Matter
 

Use of AI tools.—The constructions and their proofs—the single-determinant H1H^{1} completeness argument, the logarithmic-deletion proof of the fixed two-determinant H2H^{2} theorem variant, and the supporting codimension—were developed through extended technical exchange with ChatGPT 5.6 (Pro and Sol) and Claude Opus 4.8. The same tools implemented the numerical cross-checks of both theorems (the capacity-cost, incidence, and logarithmic-deletion tests) and ran a multi-agent adversarial audit that re-derived the load-bearing steps and independently verified the bibliography; the schematic figures were generated with Matplotlib code written by Claude Fable 5, as disclosed in the figure captions. They, together with Claude Fable 5, also assisted in drafting and revising the text. The Authors checked and curated every definition, statement, proof, and numerical result, and take full responsibility for the content of the paper.

Supplemental Material for “A Fixed Universal Determinant is Variationally Complete for Continuum Fermions”

Giuseppe Carleo1,2 and Riccardo Rossi1,2,3

3CNRS, Laboratoire de Physique Théorique de la Matière Condensée, Sorbonne Université, 75005 Paris, France

This document contains the proof of the following Theorem, which was presented in the main text of the manuscript, whose statement we reproduce below.

Theorem 1.

Let s∈{1,2}s\in\{1,2\}. If ψ∈H−s​(ℝd×N)\psi\in H^{s}_{-}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}) is a spinless fermionic wave function of NN particles in dd spatial dimensions, it exists a finite set of sequences of smooth compactly-supported bosonic NN-particle wave functions ϕα,n∈Cc,+∞​(ℝd×N)\phi_{\alpha,n}\in C^{\infty}_{c,+}(\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}) such that

limn→∞‖ψ−∑α=1Ks(d)𝒟α(d)​ϕα,n‖Hs=0,\lim_{n\to\infty}\left\lVert\psi-\sum_{\alpha=1}^{K_{s}^{(d)}}\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}^{(d)}\,\phi_{\alpha,n}\right\rVert_{H^{s}}=0, (S1)

where 𝒟α(d)\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}^{(d)} are universal, ψ\psi-independent, antisymmetric polynomials in the particle coordinates. We show that K1(d)=1K_{1}^{(d)}=1 for d∈{1,2,3}d\in\{1,2,3\}, K2(d)=1K_{2}^{(d)}=1 for d∈{1,2}d\in\{1,2\}, and K2(3)≤2K_{2}^{(3)}\leq 2.

S1 Statement and notation

Set

𝒳d,N:=(ℝd)N≅ℝd​N,X=(x1,…,xN).\mathcal{X}_{d,N}:=(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{N}\cong\mathbb{R}^{dN},\qquad X=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}).

For σ∈SN\sigma\in S_{N}, define

σ​X=(xσ−1​(1),…,xσ−1​(N)).\sigma X=(x_{\sigma^{-1}(1)},\ldots,x_{\sigma^{-1}(N)}).

The symmetric and antisymmetric Sobolev spaces are

H+s​(𝒳d,N)\displaystyle H^{s}_{+}(\mathcal{X}_{d,N}) ={ϕ∈Hs:ϕ⁡(σ​X)=ϕ⁡(X)​ for every ​σ∈SN},\displaystyle=\{\phi\in H^{s}:\phi(\sigma X)=\phi(X)\text{ for every }\sigma\in S_{N}\},
H−s​(𝒳d,N)\displaystyle H^{s}_{-}(\mathcal{X}_{d,N}) ={ψ∈Hs:ψ⁡(σ​X)=sgn⁡(σ)​ψ​(X)​ for every ​σ∈SN}.\displaystyle=\{\psi\in H^{s}:\psi(\sigma X)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\psi(X)\text{ for every }\sigma\in S_{N}\}.

All functions are complex-valued, as is natural for Schroedinger wave functions.

For a real-linear map p:ℝd→ℂp:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{C}, define the projected Vandermonde

Δp​(X):=∏1≤i<j≤N(p⁡(xi)−p⁡(xj)).\Delta_{p}(X):=\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\bigl(p(x_{i})-p(x_{j})\bigr). (S2)

Since a permutation only reorders the factors with the usual Vandermonde sign,

Δp​(σ​X)=sgn⁡(σ)​Δp​(X).\Delta_{p}(\sigma X)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\Delta_{p}(X). (S3)

We use the following fixed choices.

  • •

    If d=1d=1,

    𝒟1(1)​(X)=Δ⁡(X):=∏i<j(xi−xj).\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(1)}(X)=\Delta(X):=\prod_{i<j}(x_{i}-x_{j}).
  • •

    If d≥2d\geq 2,

    p1​(x)=x(1)+i​x(2),𝒟1(d)=Δp1.p_{1}(x)=x^{(1)}+ix^{(2)},\qquad\mathcal{D}_{1}^{(d)}=\Delta_{p_{1}}.
  • •

    If d=3d=3,

    p2​(x)=x(2)+i​x(3),𝒟2(3)=Δp2.p_{2}(x)=x^{(2)}+ix^{(3)},\qquad\mathcal{D}_{2}^{(3)}=\Delta_{p_{2}}.

The proof of the theorem is straightforward once the deletion lemma is proven in Sec. S3.

S2 Reduction to smooth compactly-supported fermionic functions

Define the antisymmetrizer

(P−​u)​(X):=1N!​∑σ∈SNsgn⁡(σ)​u​(σ−1​X).(P_{-}u)(X):=\frac{1}{N!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{N}}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)u(\sigma^{-1}X). (S4)

Every permutation acts isometrically on Hs​(𝒳d,N)H^{s}(\mathcal{X}_{d,N}), hence P−P_{-} is a bounded projection on HsH^{s}.

Lemma 2.

For every integer s≥0s\geq 0,

Cc,−∞​(𝒳d,N):=Cc∞​(𝒳d,N)∩H−s​(𝒳d,N)C_{c,-}^{\infty}(\mathcal{X}_{d,N}):=C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{X}_{d,N})\cap H^{s}_{-}(\mathcal{X}_{d,N})

is dense in H−s​(𝒳d,N)H^{s}_{-}(\mathcal{X}_{d,N}).

Proof.

Take ψ∈H−s\psi\in H^{s}_{-}. Since Cc∞​(𝒳d,N)C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{X}_{d,N}) is dense in Hs​(𝒳d,N)H^{s}(\mathcal{X}_{d,N}), choose un∈Cc∞u_{n}\in C_{c}^{\infty} with un→ψu_{n}\to\psi in HsH^{s}. Then P−​un∈Cc,−∞P_{-}u_{n}\in C_{c,-}^{\infty} and

‖P−​un−ψ‖Hs=‖P−​(un−ψ)‖Hs≤‖P−‖​‖un−ψ‖Hs⟶0,\|P_{-}u_{n}-\psi\|_{H^{s}}=\|P_{-}(u_{n}-\psi)\|_{H^{s}}\leq\|P_{-}\|\,\|u_{n}-\psi\|_{H^{s}}\longrightarrow 0,

because P−​ψ=ψP_{-}\psi=\psi. ∎

It is therefore enough to start with a fixed f∈Cc,−∞f\in C_{c,-}^{\infty} and approximate this ff by the required factorizations.

S3 The logarithmic cutoff lemma

The nodal sets of the projected Vandermonde determinants are finite unions of linear subspaces. At the critical Sobolev codimension, to be introduced below, an ordinary cutoff is too expensive. We show instead that a logarithmic cutoff has vanishing Sobolev cost.

S3.1 A regularized distance to a finite union of subspaces

Let

Z=⋃ν=1JLν⊂ℝM,Z=\bigcup_{\nu=1}^{J}L_{\nu}\subset\mathbb{R}^{M},

where each LνL_{\nu} is a linear subspace. Put

δν​(X):=dist⁡(X,Lν),δ⁡(X):=dist⁡(X,Z)=minν⁡δν​(X).\delta_{\nu}(X):=\operatorname{dist}(X,L_{\nu}),\qquad\delta(X):=\operatorname{dist}(X,Z)=\min_{\nu}\delta_{\nu}(X).

For X∉ZX\notin Z, define

ρ(X):=(∑ν=1Jδν(X)−2)−1/2.\rho(X):=\left(\sum_{\nu=1}^{J}\delta_{\nu}(X)^{-2}\right)^{-1/2}. (S5)

Then

δ⁡(X)J≤ρ⁡(X)≤δ⁡(X).\frac{\delta(X)}{\sqrt{J}}\leq\rho(X)\leq\delta(X). (S6)

Indeed, if δ=minν⁡δν\delta=\min_{\nu}\delta_{\nu}, then

δ−2≤∑νδν−2≤J​δ−2,\delta^{-2}\leq\sum_{\nu}\delta_{\nu}^{-2}\leq J\delta^{-2},

and taking inverse square roots gives (S6).

Let PνP_{\nu} be the orthogonal projection onto Lν⟂L_{\nu}^{\perp}. Then δν​(X)2=|Pν​X|2\delta_{\nu}(X)^{2}=|P_{\nu}X|^{2}. Differentiating (S5) gives the pointwise estimates

|D​ρ​(X)|≤C,|D2​ρ​(X)|≤Cρ⁡(X),X∉Z.|D\rho(X)|\leq C,\qquad|D^{2}\rho(X)|\leq\frac{C}{\rho(X)},\qquad X\notin Z. (S7)

For completeness, write

R(X):=∑νδν(X)−2,ρ=R−1/2.R(X):=\sum_{\nu}\delta_{\nu}(X)^{-2},\qquad\rho=R^{-1/2}.

Since

|D⁡(δν−2)|≤C​δν−3,|D2​(δν−2)|≤C​δν−4,|D(\delta_{\nu}^{-2})|\leq C\delta_{\nu}^{-3},\qquad|D^{2}(\delta_{\nu}^{-2})|\leq C\delta_{\nu}^{-4},

and δν≥ρ\delta_{\nu}\geq\rho, one obtains

|D​R|≤C​ρ−3,|D2​R|≤C​ρ−4.|DR|\leq C\rho^{-3},\qquad|D^{2}R|\leq C\rho^{-4}.

Now

Dρ=−12R−3/2DR,D\rho=-\frac{1}{2}R^{-3/2}DR,

and

D2ρ=34R−5/2DR⊗DR−12R−3/2D2R.D^{2}\rho=\frac{3}{4}R^{-5/2}DR\otimes DR-\frac{1}{2}R^{-3/2}D^{2}R.

Using R=ρ−2R=\rho^{-2} gives (S7).

Suppose that every LνL_{\nu} has codimension at least qq. On every fixed compact set K⊂ℝMK\subset\mathbb{R}^{M}, the tubular-neighborhood estimate

|K∩{ρ<t}|≤CKtq,0<t<1,\bigl|K\cap\{\rho<t\}\bigr|\leq C_{K}t^{q},\qquad 0<t<1, (S8)

holds. To see this, use (S6):

{ρ<t}⊂{δ<Jt}⊂⋃ν=1J{δν<Jt}.\{\rho<t\}\subset\{\delta<\sqrt{J}t\}\subset\bigcup_{\nu=1}^{J}\{\delta_{\nu}<\sqrt{J}t\}.

Ia(ε):=∫K∩{ε2<ρ<ε}ρ−adX≤{C​εq−a,a<q,C​|log⁡ε|,a=q.I_{a}(\varepsilon):=\int_{K\cap\{\varepsilon^{2}<\rho<\varepsilon\}}\rho^{-a}\,dX\leq\begin{cases}C\varepsilon^{q-a},&a<q,\\ C|\log\varepsilon|,&a=q.\end{cases} (S9)

S3.2 The cutoff and its derivatives

Fix θ∈C∞​(ℝ)\theta\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) such that

0≤θ≤1,θ⁡(t)=0​ for ​t≤0,θ⁡(t)=1​ for ​t≥1.0\leq\theta\leq 1,\qquad\theta(t)=0\text{ for }t\leq 0,\qquad\theta(t)=1\text{ for }t\geq 1.

Lemma 3 (Logarithmic deletion lemma).

Let ZZ be a finite union of linear subspaces of ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M}, each of codimension at least qq, and let u∈Cc∞​(ℝM)u\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{M}).

  1. 1.

    If q≥2q\geq 2, then

    u​χε⟶uin ​H1​(ℝM).u\chi_{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow u\quad\text{in }H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{M}).
  2. 2.

    If q≥4q\geq 4, then

    u​χε⟶uin ​H2​(ℝM).u\chi_{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow u\quad\text{in }H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{M}).
  3. 3.

    If q≥2q\geq 2 and u=0u=0 on ZZ, then

    u​χε⟶uin ​H2​(ℝM).u\chi_{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow u\quad\text{in }H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{M}).

If ZZ is invariant under particle permutations, then χε\chi_{\varepsilon} may be chosen symmetric.

Proof.

Let

wε:=u−u​χε=u⁡(1−χε).w_{\varepsilon}:=u-u\chi_{\varepsilon}=u(1-\chi_{\varepsilon}).

All terms without derivatives of χε\chi_{\varepsilon} are supported in {ρ<ε}\{\rho<\varepsilon\} and converge to zero in L2L^{2} by (S8). We only estimate the terms containing derivatives of χε\chi_{\varepsilon}.

For H1H^{1},

∇wε=(1−χε)Du−u∇χε.\nabla w_{\varepsilon}=(1-\chi_{\varepsilon})Du-u\nabla\chi_{\varepsilon}.

Using (S12) and (S9),

∥u∇χε∥L22≤CLε2∫{ε2<ρ<ε}ρ−2dX.\|u\nabla\chi_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\frac{C}{L_{\varepsilon}^{2}}\int_{\{\varepsilon^{2}<\rho<\varepsilon\}}\rho^{-2}\,dX.

If q=2q=2, the right-hand side is O⁡(Lε−1)O(L_{\varepsilon}^{-1}). If q>2q>2, it is O⁡(εq−2​Lε−2)O(\varepsilon^{q-2}L_{\varepsilon}^{-2}). This proves part (i).

For H2H^{2},

∇⊗∇wε=(1−χε)∇⊗∇u−2sym(∇u⊗∇χε)−u∇⊗∇χε.\nabla\otimes\nabla w_{\varepsilon}=(1-\chi_{\varepsilon})\nabla\otimes\nabla u-2\,\operatorname{sym}(\nabla u\otimes\nabla\chi_{\varepsilon})-u\nabla\otimes\nabla\chi_{\varepsilon}. (S13)

The middle term satisfies

‖∇u⊗∇χε‖L22≤CLε2​I2​(ε).\|\nabla u\otimes\nabla\chi_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\frac{C}{L_{\varepsilon}^{2}}I_{2}(\varepsilon).

∥u∇⊗∇χε∥L22≤CLε2I4(ε).\|u\nabla\otimes\nabla\chi_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\frac{C}{L_{\varepsilon}^{2}}I_{4}(\varepsilon).

For q=4q=4, this is O⁡(Lε−1)O(L_{\varepsilon}^{-1}); for q>4q>4, it is O⁡(εq−4​Lε−2)O(\varepsilon^{q-4}L_{\varepsilon}^{-2}). This proves part (ii).

Now suppose u=0u=0 on ZZ. Since uu is smooth and compactly supported, it is Lipschitz. Therefore

|u⁡(X)|≤C​dist⁡(X,Z)≤C​J​ρ​(X),|u(X)|\leq C\operatorname{dist}(X,Z)\leq C\sqrt{J}\,\rho(X),

where the last inequality follows from (S6). Consequently,

|u∇⊗∇χε|≤CLε​ρ,|u\nabla\otimes\nabla\chi_{\varepsilon}|\leq\frac{C}{L_{\varepsilon}\rho},

and hence

∥u∇⊗∇χε∥L22≤CLε2I2(ε).\|u\nabla\otimes\nabla\chi_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\frac{C}{L_{\varepsilon}^{2}}I_{2}(\varepsilon).

The same bound holds for the middle term in (S13). It tends to zero for every q≥2q\geq 2, with the critical value q=2q=2 giving O⁡(Lε−1)O(L_{\varepsilon}^{-1}). This proves part (iii).

Finally, if the collection {Lν}\{L_{\nu}\} is permutation invariant, then the sum in (S5) is permutation invariant. Thus ρ\rho and χε\chi_{\varepsilon} are symmetric. ∎

S4 The one-dimensional case: exact smooth divisibility

Assume d=1d=1 and set

Δ⁡(X)=∏i<j(xi−xj).\Delta(X)=\prod_{i<j}(x_{i}-x_{j}).

In this case the factorization is exact on the smooth fermionic core.

Proposition 4.

For every Ψ∈Cc,−∞​(ℝN)\Psi\in C_{c,-}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N}), there exists Φ∈Cc,+∞​(ℝN)\Phi\in C_{c,+}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) such that

Ψ=Δ​Φ.\Psi=\Delta\Phi.
Proof.

Fix a pair i<ji<j and introduce

R=xi+xj2,r=xi−xj.R=\frac{x_{i}+x_{j}}{2},\qquad r=x_{i}-x_{j}.

Keeping all other variables fixed, antisymmetry under the transposition (i​j)(ij) gives

Ψ⁡(R,r)=−Ψ⁡(R,−r).\Psi(R,r)=-\Psi(R,-r).

In particular, Ψ⁡(R,0)=0\Psi(R,0)=0. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives the smooth Hadamard factorization

Ψ⁡(R,r)=r​∫01∂rΨ⁡(R,t​r)​𝑑t.\Psi(R,r)=r\int_{0}^{1}\partial_{r}\Psi(R,tr)\,dt. (S14)

Thus Ψ\Psi is smoothly divisible by xi−xjx_{i}-x_{j}.

Apply this argument successively to all pair hyperplanes. Dividing by one factor does not destroy vanishing on another pair hyperplane: away from the intersection of the two hyperplanes this is immediate, and continuity extends the vanishing to the intersection. Therefore

Φ:=Ψ∏i<j(xi−xj)\Phi:=\frac{\Psi}{\prod_{i<j}(x_{i}-x_{j})}

extends to a globally smooth function.

Away from the collision set,

Φ⁡(σ​X)=Ψ⁡(σ​X)Δ⁡(σ​X)=sgn⁡(σ)​Ψ​(X)sgn⁡(σ)​Δ​(X)=Φ⁡(X).\Phi(\sigma X)=\frac{\Psi(\sigma X)}{\Delta(\sigma X)}=\frac{\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\Psi(X)}{\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\Delta(X)}=\Phi(X).

By continuity, Φ\Phi is symmetric everywhere. Since Ψ\Psi is compactly supported and Φ\Phi vanishes outside the same compact set, Φ∈Cc,+∞\Phi\in C_{c,+}^{\infty}. ∎

This proves Theorem 1 for d=1d=1 in both H1H^{1} and H2H^{2}.

S5 One factor in H1H^{1} for every d≥2d\geq 2

Let

Remark 5.

The use of the complex projection x(1)+i​x(2)x^{(1)}+ix^{(2)} is essential. A real one-coordinate Vandermonde has a codimension-one nodal set in d>1d>1, and such a set cannot be deleted at arbitrarily small H1H^{1} cost.
